predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract (and Conclusion) vs. Sec. 4.1 Implementation details / Appendix "Latency between motion input and video output"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract claims "achieving true real-time generation at 30 FPS", but the implementation section states "After distillation, our method can achieve 8 FPS to generate the desired results" and the appendix reports "approximately 119 milliseconds per generated-frame, corresponding to about 8.4 FPS". The headline 30 FPS figure is contradicted by the paper's own measurements.

The Rodrigues rotation formula is written as R = I + sinθ·[u]_× + (1 + cosθ)·[u]_×^2. The correct form is R = I + sinθ·[u]_× + (1 − cosθ)·[u]_×^2. With the stated (1 + cosθ) coefficient, R is not a rotation matrix (e.g., for θ = 0 it gives I + 2[u]_×^2 ≠ I), so the derived camera extrinsics would be invalid.

The noising equation "zt = αt z0 + βt δt ε" introduces an undefined coefficient βt while the accompanying constraint is stated only for αt and δt ("αt^2 + δt^2 = 1"), so the variance-preserving property does not hold as written. Additionally, the expectation is taken over t∼U(0,1) (continuous) while the text immediately says "t = 1, …, T" (discrete denoising steps), an internally inconsistent formulation.

The benchmark is described as "100 videos collected from the Nymeria [25] dataset, which is not included for training", yet Table 1 explicitly lists Nymeria [24] (1,200 sequences) among the datasets "used for training our PlayerOne". Either the benchmark overlaps the training data (leakage) or the training table is wrong; as written the two statements contradict each other.

The metrics paragraph states that "PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS are employed" and that "we calculate the frame consistency", but no table anywhere in the paper reports SSIM or a frame-consistency score. Conversely, all tables report FVD, which is never introduced or defined in the metrics description.

The full model (CUT3R rendering) is reported as 127.16 MPJPE / 163.62 MRRPE / 50.3 PSNR / 236.12 FVD in Table 18 and Table 19 (ratio 10), but the same configuration is reported as 127.16 / 151.62 / 52.6 / 226.12 in Tables 2, 3, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14 and 15. The same model cannot have two different score sets on the same benchmark.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix "Investigation on the impact of filtering" vs. Table 19
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text claims "increasing the filtering ratio leads to a decline in model performance" and that "a filtering ratio of 10% optimizes performance". Table 19 shows the opposite for the motion/perceptual metrics: MPJPE (123.50 at 0% vs 127.16 at 10%), MRRPE (158.10 vs 163.62) and LPIPS (0.0587 vs 0.0663) are all best with no filtering, directly contradicting the stated conclusion and the earlier main-text claim that "our designed filtering strategy maximizes performance".

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 8 and surrounding text (Appendix, autonomous-driving comparison)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 8 cites "GEM [8]" and "VISTA [15]", but reference [8] is Gao et al., "VISTA: A Generalizable Driving World Model" and reference [15] is Hassan et al., "GEM: A Generalizable Ego-Vision Multimodal World Model". The two citations are swapped.

Qwen2.5-VL is cited to reference [2], "Qwen Technical Report, arXiv:2309.16609, 2023", which is the original Qwen LLM technical report, not Qwen2.5-VL (a 2025 vision-language model). The reference does not support the tool actually used for caption enrichment.

The claim "MuZero [39] runs the self-play of Monte Carlo tree search to build world models for Atari" is attributed to reference [39], which is "MuZero General: Open reimplementation of MuZero" (a GitHub repository by Duvaud & Hainaut), not the original MuZero paper by Schrittwieser et al. The scientific claim is attributed to a third-party code re-implementation.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction ("completely solves ... eliminates all limitations") and Conclusion ("coherent world generation across all scenarios without exception")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: These absolute claims are contradicted by the paper's own Limitations sections, which report degraded performance in game scenarios, failures in "highly dynamic scenes", and no physical-interaction modeling ("hands or body parts penetrating objects"). They also contradict Table 14 (game scenes worse than real) and Table 2's own qualifier of indoor-only evaluation.

The paper admits an unequal conditioning protocol: competitors are driven by (LLM-enriched) text captions while "PlayerOne directly uses motion sequences, providing it with more precise control signals". Motion-alignment metrics (MPJPE/MRRPE) and the 'Alignment' user-study score are then compared across methods, so the reported large margins over Cosmos/Aether are confounded by the input signal rather than model quality.

predicted_errors.error_location: Sec. 4.3 User study vs. Appendix "Definition of evaluation criteria"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The main text says "we let 20 annotators rate 25 groups of videos" and defines "Alignment" as "the alignment with the given text descriptions". The appendix instead states annotators "viewed both the generated video and the motion condition signal ... for all 100 videos" and defines Alignment as following the pose/motion signal. The number of rated items and the criterion definition contradict each other.

predicted_errors.error_location: Sec. 4.1 Benchmark vs. Appendix "Evaluation on Nymeria" (Tables 5, 6)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The main text describes a benchmark of 100 Nymeria videos, while the appendix says "we selected 100 videos featuring full-body actions from the test sets of four different datasets: EgoExo-4D, Nymeria, FT-HID, EgoExo-Fitness", yet Tables 5 and 6 are still captioned as evaluations "on the Nymeria dataset"/"constructed with the Nymeria dataset". The benchmark composition is described inconsistently.

Both tables claim to report competitor results on the Nymeria-based benchmark, but the numbers differ (Aether: 38.0/64.2/415.70/431.05 in Table 3 vs 37.50/63.80/418.91/435.24 in Table 6; Cosmos-14B: 51.6/79.7/256.73 vs 51.30/80.00/259.17). Similarly PlayerOne is 64.87/85.79 in Table 5 but 64.80/85.70 in Table 6. No explanation is given for the differing values.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 2, last row "PlayerOne (ours, indoor scenes only)"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The full-model row in Table 2 is labelled "indoor scenes only", yet the identical numbers (67.8/88.2/127.16/151.62/52.6/226.12/0.0663) are reported as the general full-benchmark PlayerOne result in Tables 3, 7–11, 13–15 and as the "Real" domain result in Table 14. Either the label or the reuse of these numbers as full-benchmark results is wrong; it also undermines the paper's claim of evaluation on "diverse scenarios".

Reported PSNR values (35.6 for an unfine-tuned baseline up to 56.0 dB for the 14B model) are implausible for open-ended generated video and are mutually inconsistent with the accompanying LPIPS (0.05–0.14) and FVD (180–440) values: >50 dB PSNR implies near pixel-perfect reconstruction, which cannot coexist with FVD above 200 and LPIPS above 0.05.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 18 vs. Appendix overview and "Investigation on the impact of rendering"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The appendix overview promises "Robustness to point-map rendering backends (DUSt3R / MonST3R / MASt3R; Tab. 18)" and the text says the comparison extends the DUSt3R analysis, but Table 18 contains only CUT3R, MonST3R and MASt3R — the DUSt3R row referenced in the text is absent.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix "Investigation on the impact of component division" vs. Table 16
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text claims gains "saturate after part-4/5", yet Table 16 shows continued improvement from 3 to 6 parts (DINO 62.50→63.00; MPJPE 156.76→152.62), and the deployed model uses only 3 parts — i.e., the chosen configuration is not the best in the table and the claimed saturation point does not match the reported numbers.

predicted_errors.error_location: Sec. 2 Related Work, description of The Matrix [7]
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The related-work section states that WorldMem [41] and The Matrix [7] propose "the first world simulator capable of generating infinitely long real-scene video streams with real-time, responsive control", while the Introduction and Appendix classify the very same references [10, 41, 7] as game-like simulators that "fail to accurately replicate real-world scenarios". The two characterizations of the same works are contradictory, and crediting both papers with a single 'first' claim is misattributed.

The Nymeria paper (Ma et al., ECCV 2024) is listed twice as two distinct references ([24] and [25]) and cited inconsistently (Table 1 uses [24], the benchmark section uses [25]), which makes the training/benchmark data provenance ambiguous.

The caption explains that "'Quality' particularly refers to the image resolution", but no 'Quality' row/column exists in the table; the table instead has a row labelled 'Resolution'. The caption does not match the table content.
